title: Raga Majh
hookLine: a raga with Punjabi folk roots (ang 94), full of longing

cards: Some ragas sound like a palace. This one, tradition says, sounds like a village.
In the heart of the Punjab, between the Beas and the Ravi rivers, lies the country called the Majha, and Sikh tradition links the raga's name to that land and its songs.
Turn to ang ninety-four of the Guru Granth Sahib and there it is, right after Sri Rag, at the head of its own long section.

teach.h: MAJH: A RAGA WITH DUST ON ITS FEET.
teach.b: Majh is a raga with dust on its feet. Some musicians say it grew from the folk singing of the Punjab rather than the old classical treatises, and that its home is the field and the courtyard more than the court.

teach.h: THE MOOD: LONGING ACROSS A DISTANCE.
teach.b: Whatever its exact road, the mood tradition hears in it is longing: a voice calling across a distance to someone who isn't here yet. The sound of missing. It sits right after Sri Rag's gravity.
Open the section and the first hymn isn't Guru Nanak's but Guru Ram Das's. It begins, in paraphrase: the Lord's Name has become dear to my mind; by great good fortune I've come to meditate on it.
Already it's the language of love: a thing becomes dear, fortune brings it near.

teach.h: IT OPENS WITH GURU RAM DAS.
teach.b: The section goes on with hymns of Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan, and Guru Nanak's var in Majh, a long ballad of stanzas and saloks. Why take a raga with country roots into scripture, and put it near the front?
The Granth doesn't explain its choices. But the effect is easy to hear. The divine isn't only praised in the grand voice of Sri Rag.

It's also longed for in the plain voice of home, the tune of a song someone might sing while working, missing a person far away. A listener who grew up with that sound can hear scripture in their own accent.
Tomorrow, one hymn in Majh, and the longing gets a story.

how: Ragis sing shabads from the Majh section in Raag Majh, and its compositions, including Guru Nanak's Majh ki Var, are read in the Guru Granth Sahib in the order the Granth gives them.

o: a raga of longing from the Punjab's heartland
a grand court raga, sung for kings and nobles
a fast raga kept for festival dancing at harvest

p: Guru Ram Das: the Name made dear

games.q: you're setting a hymn about missing the beloved for people raised on village songs. which voice do you give it?
o: the grand voice of the court.
a tune with the sound of home in it.
games.why: Majh, which tradition ties to the Punjab's own country, sits right after Sri Rag, so longing for the divine can be heard in the accent of home.

practice: If you can find a shabad sung in Raag Majh, play it and listen for the reaching in the melody, the way a phrase leans out toward something and comes back.

If not, bring to mind someone you miss, far away, out of touch, or gone, and let the missing sit beside you without pushing the feeling up or down. If you pray, hold that person, and the longing itself, inside one quiet Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Raga Majh. The second raga section of the Granth, opening on ang ninety-four with Guru Ram Das, named by tradition for a region of the Punjab, and heard as a raga of longing. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Majh, the raga of the Granth's second section; tradition links it to the Majha region of the Punjab.

carryVoice: Your line: punjabi longing. Scripture, sung in the plain voice of home and field. See you tomorrow.
